name: Writing Support
title: Writing Support
answer: Writing support for English learners and newcomers uses AI as a language resource under teacher guidance. The teacher shapes when and how students use their home language and the tool together, while the student remains the writer. This matters because the text reports gains in academic literacy, pronunciation, and motivation when teacher mediation is present, and it warns that assessment is where errors cause the most harm.

sections.body: Writing in an additional language places heavy demands on a student, and this idea addresses that demand by placing AI inside a teacher-shaped routine. The tool can help with specific words or structures while the student remains the writer. Planned use of the student's home language is part of the support, not a workaround. The problem it solves is that a tool alone does not create academic literacy or motivation. Teacher mediation is what turns the tool into useful writing support.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the text's secondary example, students learning Spanish used generative AI with teacher guidance and planned home-language use. A bilingual writing routine might have a student brainstorm in the home language, then write in English while the tool helps with particular words or structures. The student remains the writer, while the tool serves as a language resource. Reliance on the tool is expected to decrease over time, following the same fade principle as translation. The text also describes teachers using ChatGPT to communicate with multilingual learners, differentiate materials, and build scaffolds.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports a study of 48 immigrant secondary students learning Spanish. Generative AI used with teacher guidance and planned use of students' home languages improved academic literacy, pronunciation, and motivation over eight weeks (de Amo Sanchez-Fortun, 2026). It also reports observations of 42 teachers who used ChatGPT to communicate with multilingual learners, differentiate materials, and build scaffolds (Donley, 2024). The same study noted gaps in how teachers used AI for assessment and reflection.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Teacher mediation, rather than the tool by itself, is described as the key. Students receive instruction on when and how to combine their home language with the AI. The student remains the writer, while the tool serves as a language resource, and reliance is expected to fade over time. The text also points to gaps in teachers' use of AI for assessment and reflection, and it warns that assessment is where errors do the most harm. Decisions about when and how to use the tool stay with the teacher.
